title: Spatially constrained clustering of urban morphology for solar and wind performance assessment: The case of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia
content:
by Wondwosen Debebe Mekonnen, Tibebu Assefa Woldeamanuel

Addis Ababa, a rapidly growing city in sub-Saharan Africa, is characterized by spontaneous and unplanned urban development, making it challenging to derive simplified spatial models for sustainable urban analysis. This study examines urban morphological clusters based on building height and footprint characteristics and investigates their relationships with solar and wind performance indicators. The methodology comprised four analytical stages. First, spatially constrained hierarchical clustering was performed in GeoDa to classify urban morphology using relevant building variables, resulting in 31 morphological clusters across 861 boundary units. Second, a statistically and spatially robust sampling procedure identified 92 representative samples. Third, solar and wind performance indicators were computed. Fourth, the performance indicators were validated using Grasshopper–Rhino with Ladybug for solar performance and ANSYS Fluent for wind performance. Regression analysis was subsequently conducted to evaluate statistically significant relationships among morphological and performance indicators. For solar performance, ground space index and façade-to-site ratio exhibited negative relationships with façade solar irradiation, whereas sky view factor showed a positive relationship. For wind performance, displacement height was negatively associated with block-scale wind performance. A positive relationship was also identified between façade solar irradiation and wind velocity magnitude. The proposed approach provides a systematic means of extracting meaningful relationships between urban morphology and environmental performance in cities lacking well-defined spatial models, thereby supporting evidence-based sustainable urban development.
